claim: Coughlin et al. 2019 is the only published Gravity Spy method evaluated as a one-reference similarity search: a single known glitch is the query and the metric is the fraction of the archive that can be discarded while retaining 50% (or 100%) of the known examples of that class.
title: Classifying the unknown: discovering novel gravitational-wave detector glitches using similarity learning (Coughlin et al., PRD 99, 082002)
relevance: This is the comparison HyperNet should cite. To compare, compute on TEST the same 'archive fraction rejected at 50% recall' per class; HyperNet's recall-at-1%-false-alarm (48.7%) is approximately the same operating point (99% rejection, ~50% retention) and so is directly comparable to DIRECT's ~99% rejection at 50% retention on Water Jet, and to raw pixels' ~30%.

claim: The DIRECT similarity model behind Gravity Spy's search is not label-free: it is ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 plus a 1024-unit and a 200-unit layer, trained with a pairwise contrastive (margin) loss on labeled same-class/different-class pairs from the Gravity Spy training set, and queried with cosine distance.
title: DIRECT: Deep Discriminative Embedding for Clustering of LIGO Data (Bahaadini et al., ICIP 2018)
relevance: HyperNet's no-real-labels, no-pretrained-weights constraint is strictly tighter than any published Gravity Spy similarity method. State this explicitly when comparing numbers; DIRECT uses both ImageNet weights and 16-22 labeled classes.

claim: On the easy novel class (Raven Peck) raw pixels and PCA match the learned DIRECT embedding; the learned embedding only wins on the class whose defining feature is subtle and absent from the training classes (Water Jet).
title: Christopher Berry blog summary of Classifying the unknown (Raven Pecks and Water Jets)
relevance: Independent confirmation that raw pixels are a strong baseline on fixed-axis Gravity Spy spectrograms (HyperNet's 0.485 mAP). A v0.4 evaluation should report per-class gains over raw pixels and look specifically at subtle-feature classes; a uniform small gain is less convincing than winning where pixels fail.

claim: DIRECT's held-out-class clustering score on Gravity Spy v1.0 is NMI 0.5978 / ARI 0.4550 with k-means on 5 unseen classes, versus raw features NMI 0.5131 / ARI 0.1986, PCA 0.5117 / 0.1938 and a deep autoencoder 0.5451 / 0.3243.
title: DIRECT: Deep Discriminative Embedding for Clustering of LIGO Data
relevance: Gives a secondary, label-free-at-test metric (NMI/ARI of k-means on HyperNet features over held-out classes) that HyperNet could add cheaply to v0.4 to compare against DIRECT, VAT and CTSAE; raw-feature NMI around 0.43-0.51 is the floor to beat.

claim: The 2022 VAT-based discriminative model improves held-out-class clustering NMI to 0.61 versus DIRECT 0.53 and raw features / PCA 0.43, training on the first 10 of 22 classes of Gravity Spy v1.2 (7,932 glitches) and clustering the remaining 10.
title: Discriminative Dimensionality Reduction using Deep Neural Networks for Clustering of LIGO data (Bahaadini, Wu, Coughlin, Zevin, Katsaggelos)
relevance: Shows the semi-supervised route (unlabeled in-domain spectrograms via VAT smoothing) is what moved the field past DIRECT. Relevant to open problem (4): if HyperNet allows unlabeled in-domain pretraining, this is the published precedent and the number to compare against.

claim: CTSAE (2024) is the first fully unsupervised glitch clusterer on Gravity Spy O3 (41,745 glitches, 23 classes, 224x224 resized from 480x575, four durations) and reaches ARI 0.4091 / NMI 0.6362, beating DIRECT (0.2137 / 0.4281) and VAT with 1% labels (0.4054 / 0.5963) but not VAT with 5% labels (0.5938 / 0.7011); the authors avoid augmentation-based contrastive learning because 'Augmenting glitch spectrograms can significantly distort their physical semantics.'
title: Cross-Temporal Spectrogram Autoencoder (CTSAE): Unsupervised Dimensionality Reduction for Clustering Gravitational Wave Glitches (Li, Wu, Katsaggelos)
relevance: Two design lessons: (1) DIRECT's score collapses on O3 data, so a label-trained embedding does not transfer across observing runs, which supports testing HyperNet on O3 as fresh data; (2) the domain's practitioners judge standard SimCLR-style augmentations to be physically unsafe on spectrograms, which bears on how HyperNet should design synthetic 'two views of the same type' pairs (vary instance, not geometry).

claim: The original Gravity Spy CNN (Zevin et al. 2017) reached 97.1% test accuracy on 7,718 glitches in 20 classes using four merged Omega scans (0.5, 1, 2, 4 s), with Wandering Line (44 samples) and Paired Doves (30 samples) having the lowest precision and recall and None of the Above / No Glitch also weak.
title: Gravity Spy: Integrating Advanced LIGO Detector Characterization, Machine Learning, and Citizen Science (Zevin et al., CQG 34, 064003)
relevance: Supervised accuracy is not comparable to one-reference mAP, but the hard-class list (Wandering Line, Paired Doves, catch-all classes) matches HyperNet's rare set and should be reported per class in v0.4.

claim: Bahaadini et al.'s multi-view models on 7,730 glitches / 20 classes used tiny inputs (47x57 per duration; merged view 94x114) and reached 96.89% (merged) vs 92.85-95.34% for single durations, with the 1 s view best among single views; hardest classes were Wandering Line (57-71%), Repeating Blips (76-80%) and Light Modulation (83-87%).
title: Deep Multi-view Models for Glitch Classification (Bahaadini et al., ICASSP 2017)
relevance: Supports HyperNet's choice of the 1.0 s view and shows useful class information survives at 47x57 resolution, consistent with 48x48 raw pixels scoring 0.485. Also suggests a cheap v0.4 upgrade: concatenate features from two durations (1 s + 4 s), which gave +1.5-4 points in supervised accuracy.

claim: George, Shen & Huerta fine-tuned ImageNet CNNs on ~8,500 Gravity Spy O1 images (22 classes, 80/20 split, 224x224 or 299x299 crops from 481x575) and reached 98.84% top-1 (ResNet50, InceptionV3) vs 96.70% for a scratch CNN; the 'few labeled examples' claim rests only on Paired_Doves (about 21-24 training images, 100% recall for most models) and the clustering experiment reports no metrics.
title: Deep Transfer Learning: A new deep learning glitch classification method for advanced LIGO (George, Shen, Huerta; PRD 97, 101501)
relevance: Not one-reference and uses ImageNet weights, so not a fair comparator; but it is the canonical evidence that natural-image pretraining transfers to glitch spectrograms, which is the hypothesis HyperNet's synthetic curriculum is trying to replace. A frozen ImageNet-CNN feature baseline (no fine-tuning) would be a fair 'upper reference' row for v0.4.

claim: The current Gravity Spy O3/O4 classifier (Wu et al. 2024) uses four 448x448 views with attention fusion on 23 O3 classes (8,439 train / 1,687 val / 3,538 test, confidence > 0.9) and scores 0.941 accuracy / 0.931 F1 vs 0.906 / 0.904 for the previous classifier; hardest classes are Wandering Line (0.740, 25 train), Paired Doves (0.882), Fast Scattering (0.890), Helix (0.891), with confusions Extremely Loud vs Koi Fish, Blip vs Repeating Blips, Scattered Light vs Low-frequency Lines.
title: Advancing Glitch Classification in Gravity Spy: Multi-view Fusion with Attention-based Machine Learning for Advanced LIGO's Fourth Observing Run (Wu, Zevin, Berry et al., CQG)
relevance: Defines the modern class list and confusion pairs; the O3 data behind it (Zenodo 5649212) is a fresh held-out source for v0.4. Flag: v2 revised Aug 2025, may be newer than training data.

claim: Gravity Spy's O1-O3 machine-learning classifications are public on Zenodo with 22 classes for O1/O2 and 23 for O3 (adds Fast_Scattering and Blip_Low_Frequency, drops None_of_the_Above), covering 233,981 Hanford and 379,805 Livingston glitches with per-class confidences and four Omega-scan durations; the O3 training set was 9,631 samples (8,427 train / 1,203 val) with 99.9% train / 98.8% validation accuracy and no test accuracy reported.
title: Gravity Spy Machine Learning Classifications of LIGO Glitches from Observing Runs O1, O2, O3a, and O3b (Glanzer et al., CQG 40, 065004)
relevance: Answers open problem (2): O3a/O3b glitches with confidence >= 0.9 give a large, never-touched test archive at realistic class imbalance; labels are machine labels, so confirm with the volunteer-classification release (Zenodo 5911227) for the reference and target sets.

claim: GSpyNetTree (2023) is a signal-vs-glitch tree of three 5-class CNNs (GW, Blip, Low-frequency Blip, No Glitch, plus Scratchy / Koi Fish / Tomte) trained on about 1,000 examples per class with four time-offset augmentations; InceptionV3 variants exceed 96% per class, but accuracy falls to about 76% under a background shift and unseen glitch classes are badly misassigned (Scattering 42% No Glitch, Thunder 85% No Glitch, Repeating Blips only 46-56% as Blip).
title: GSpyNetTree: A signal-vs-glitch classifier for gravitational-wave event candidates (Alvarez-Lopez et al., CQG)
relevance: Not a retrieval method; relevant mainly as evidence that supervised glitch CNNs do not generalize to unseen classes or shifted backgrounds, which is the argument for a one-reference recognizer. Also note the 2026 follow-ups GSpyNetTree-O4 (arXiv 2607.25208) and GSpyNetTreeS (arXiv 2511.16861), not read in full.

claim: No published 2022-2026 paper applies contrastive or SimCLR-style self-supervised pretraining to LIGO/Virgo glitch spectrograms; the closest are a 2023 pseudo-label self-supervised CNN (F1 94.15% vs 97.18% supervised on Gravity Spy), a 2026 KAGRA ConvAE/DEC clustering (NMI 0.34-0.37, ARI 0.30-0.44 vs PCA 0.22/0.17 on 2,215 events, 7 classes), and 2026 frozen-foundation-model work (DINOv2 ViT-S/14 on O4a, AST audio transformer) that report no retrieval metrics.
title: Unsupervised Morphological Characterization of Gravitational-Wave Glitches in LIGO O4a Using Frozen DINOv2 Features (Cirfeta)
relevance: The gap HyperNet targets (features better than random/raw without real labels or pretrained weights) is unoccupied in the literature. But reviewers will expect a frozen-DINOv2 or frozen-ImageNet cosine k-NN row as the 'foundation model' reference. All 2026 items are newer than training data and were read from abstracts only; verify before citing.

claim: The Gravity Spy v1.1 training set (Zenodo 1486046, 1 Nov 2018, CC BY 4.0) stores each sample as four {1,140,170} arrays (0.5, 1, 2, 4 s) in trainingsetv1d1.h5, with the plot-only crop x=[66,532], y=[105,671] applied to the raw PNGs; the v1.1 README itself does not state class or split counts.
title: Gravity Spy Training Set v1.1.0 (Coughlin, Zenodo)
relevance: Confirms HyperNet's 140x170 input and crop match the publisher's canonical preprocessing (and the v15 crop [105,66,671,532] on 800x600 images), so comparisons to Coughlin 2019 and Bahaadini 2018 are on the same pixels. The v1.1 TEST split has now been scored three times; the O3 release above is the natural replacement.

claim: Among statistical and procedural noise generators trained contrastively, flat-shape generators transfer worst and oriented/textured ones best: Dead-leaves Squares 0.35, Oriented 0.37, Shapes 0.39, Textures 0.41, Spectrum-only 0.31, Spectrum+Color 0.37, Spectrum+Color+WMM 0.40, StyleGAN-Oriented 0.43 (ImageNet-100 linear top-1, AlexNet, alignment/uniformity loss), versus real ImageNet-100 0.63 and a random CNN 0.21.
title: Learning to See by Looking at Noise (Baradad, Wulff, Wang, Isola, Torralba, NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: HyperNet's flat-colored clean shapes on simple backgrounds sit at the Dead-leaves Squares/Shapes end of this ordering, the weakest synthetic family measured; adding texture inside shapes and a 1/f-like background (the Spectrum+Color+WMM and Textures variants) is what moved the needle in this study.

claim: In Baradad et al. 2021 the properties that predicted transfer were dataset diversity (recall, r=0.83 with accuracy) and similarity of the color distribution to natural images (r=-0.57 for color distance), while matching the 1/f power spectrum was only weakly correlated with accuracy.
title: Learning to See by Looking at Noise (NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: For spectrogram transfer the analogue of 'color distribution' is the intensity/colormap statistics of Gravity Spy Q-transform images; the synthetic distribution should be rendered with the same colormap and value histogram, and should span a wide range of patterns (diversity) rather than a few shape families.

claim: Under a shared ResNet-50/MoCo-v2 protocol every synthetic dataset beats random initialization by a wide margin on ImageNet-1k linear probing: random init 4.36, Dead-leaves Mixed 20.00, FractalDB-1k 23.86, Shaders-21k 30.25, StyleGAN-Oriented 38.12, Shaders-21k+MixUp 44.83, versus Places365 55.59 and ImageNet-1k 67.50.
title: Procedural Image Programs for Representation Learning (Baradad et al., NeurIPS 2022)
relevance: No published synthetic-pretraining result shows trained features losing to random features; HyperNet's v0.1-v0.3 finding that trained blocks never beat random is an outlier that implicates the objective and the narrow drawing distribution, not synthetic pretraining as such. Note these protocols all use a linear probe with real labels, unlike HyperNet's frozen one-reference retrieval.

claim: Shaders-21k transfer scales logarithmically with the number of distinct generative programs and is not saturated at 21k; the strongest per-program predictor of poor transfer is high intra-image self-similarity (LPIPS, r=0.46), and the worst StyleGAN latent walks 'collapsed to repetitive shapes, grayscale, or solid color' while the best were colorful and filled the canvas.
title: Procedural Image Programs for Representation Learning (NeurIPS 2022)
relevance: HyperNet's shape-family renders (solid fills, simple backgrounds, repeated motifs) match the description of the lowest-performing programs; a v0.4 generator should be scored by gzip size and intra-image LPIPS self-similarity before training, and the number of independent pattern programs should be in the thousands.

claim: Supervised labels over synthetic programs help only in the mid regime (roughly 20 to 1000 programs); with 21k programs contrastive SimCLR (47.74) and SupCon (48.10) match while plain cross-entropy (40.3) falls behind, and MixUp between rendered images is what closes the gap to real data for the contrastive learner (S-21k 30.25 to 44.83 on ImageNet-1k).
title: Procedural Image Programs for Representation Learning (NeurIPS 2022)
relevance: HyperNet's family-classification head with a small number of families corresponds to the mid regime where labels help, but its InfoNCE positives are two renders of one program, so there is no cross-program mixing; MixUp-style compositing of several synthetic patterns into one image (which naturally produces overlapping glitch-like structures on a background) was the single largest lever in this paper.

claim: Shaders-21k+MixUp nearly matches real-image pretraining on VTAB Specialized (satellite/medical) tasks: 84.08 vs Places365 84.19 vs random init 54.30, with EuroSAT 92.72, Resisc45 83.68, Retinopathy 75.21 and Camelyon 84.72, and shader features beat ImageNet-1k features on dSprites orientation (18.33-19.01 vs 12.92).
title: Procedural Image Programs for Representation Learning (NeurIPS 2022)
relevance: Non-natural scientific imagery is exactly where synthetic pretraining comes closest to real pretraining, so the goal of beating random features on spectrograms is realistic in the literature; the gap in HyperNet is therefore in distribution and objective choice, not in the premise.

claim: In FractalDB the number of synthetic categories matters more than instances per category (16 to 1000 categories: +7.9 C10 / +16.0 C100; 16 to 1000 instances: +5.2 / +8.9), images must be rendered densely enough to form contours (patch rendering 92.9/73.6 vs point 87.4/66.1 on C10/C100), fill rate above ~20% hurts sharply (C100 72.3 at 0.10 vs 63.2 at 0.25), and color 'appears not to be strong'.
title: Pre-training without Natural Images (Kataoka et al., ACCV 2020 / IJCV)
relevance: HyperNet's few shape families are the wrong axis of scale: the FDSL evidence says scale the number of distinct pattern types (hundreds to thousands) and keep each type's within-class variation modest; dense, textured, moderately sparse renders beat sparse flat shapes.

claim: Contour structure, not fill or color, carries the FDSL pretraining signal for ViTs: drawing background-colored lines over RCDB images to break contours dropped fine-tuning accuracy on C10/C100/Cars/Flowers from 95.5/79.4/78.4/96.4 to 46.2/22.1/1.1/8.8; with 21k classes ExFractalDB (82.7) and RCDB (82.4) beat ImageNet-21k (81.8) on ImageNet-1k fine-tuning of ViT-B.
title: Replacing Labeled Real-image Datasets with Auto-generated Contours (Kataoka et al., CVPR 2022)
relevance: HyperNet already hands the CNN Sobel edges as a fixed input channel, so a contour-only synthetic prior adds little; Gravity Spy glitches are soft-edged energy blobs, streaks and bands in noise, where the discriminative signal is intensity profile, orientation and periodicity rather than closed contours, so the RCDB/VisualAtom recipe is a poor fit for spectrograms.

claim: VisualAtom-21k (sinusoidal-contour classes) reaches 83.7% ImageNet-1k top-1 with ViT-B at 384px versus JFT-300M 84.2% and ImageNet-21k 83.0%, and its ablations show narrowing the contour frequency range [0,20] to [20,20]-style ranges lowers every downstream score; the authors conclude 'variety of contour shapes is a crucial factor'.
title: Visual Atoms: Pre-training Vision Transformers with Sinusoidal Waves (Takashima et al., CVPR 2023)
relevance: Each VisualAtom class is a parameter DISTRIBUTION with per-image resampling of nuisance parameters, which is precisely the within-type variation the v15 scope review found missing from HyperNet's same-program positive pairs; v0.4 should define glitch-like types as parameter ranges and draw independent members.

claim: One synthetic image per category suffices when instances are replaced by augmentation: OFDB-1k (one fractal per class) fine-tunes to 84.0 vs lower FractalDB-1k, 85.3 with random-patch augmentation, and OFDB-21k (21k images) matches or exceeds ImageNet-21k (14M images) on ImageNet-1k; the ECCV 2024 follow-up shows a single fractal with parameter perturbations ('1p-frac') is on par with ImageNet-1k pretraining for full fine-tuning.
title: Pre-training Vision Transformers with Very Limited Synthesized Images (Nakamura et al., ICCV 2023); see also Scaling Backwards, ECCV 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00677
relevance: What transfers is the task of discriminating many classes under controlled augmentation, not the pixel realism or volume of the images; HyperNet's 755k-param CNN with contrastive same-program pairs does not pose a many-class discrimination problem of this kind, and these results are for fine-tuned ViTs, so they do not guarantee frozen-feature gains.

claim: For audio spectrograms, Formula-SED (harmonic stacks plus FIR-filtered uniform noise, parameter trajectories drawn from Gaussian processes, reverb, up to four mixed sources, multi-label classification of discretized synthesis parameters) pretrains a 1.1M-parameter CRNN to PSDS1 0.405 on DESED versus 0.352 from scratch and 0.387 with AudioSet-strong pretraining; scaling to 1M clips gives 0.420, and removing Mixup is the largest single augmentation loss (0.405 to 0.376).
title: Formula-Supervised Sound Event Detection: Pre-Training Without Real Data (Shibata et al., 2025; newer than my training data, verify)
relevance: This is a working spectrogram-domain FDSL recipe at HyperNet's parameter scale: time-frequency primitives with GP-smoothed parameter curves (which produce the smooth blobs, bends and bands seen in Gravity Spy), noise with time-varying filtering, and an objective that classifies the generating parameters rather than matching two views of one clip.

claim: AudioPG's cumulative ablation shows which spectrogram primitives matter: sine-only pretraining gives 42.25% ESC-50, adding harmonics 69.25, adding ADSR dynamics 73.25, adding spectral damping plus noise bursts and background noise 82.00 (50-epoch protocol); the full model fine-tunes to 90.60 ESC-50 / 0.546 FSD50K mAP vs 54.00 / 0.398 from scratch, pretraining in under 20 minutes on one GPU with a 75%-mask log-Mel MAE.
title: From Physics to Representation: Audio Learning with Synthetic Pre-training via Procedural Generation (AudioPG, 2026; newer than my training data, verify)
relevance: The biggest gain comes from noise and damping, i.e. a realistic noisy background and softened edges, exactly what HyperNet's clean flat drawings lack; multiple overlapping events per image also help. A v0.4 generator should composite 1-5 chirps/bands/blobs/bursts over a 1/f background at varied SNR.

claim: Procedural spectrogram data has far lower patch diversity and much higher temporal predictability than real audio (shared-codebook entropy: marginal 3.14 vs 6.70, temporal 0.715 vs 3.807 for FormulaBank vs AudioSet-28K), so masked-autoencoder pretraining on it needs low mask ratios (10-25%) where real audio prefers 50-75%; formula-class coverage drives FDSL gains while within-class rendering diversity drives MAE gains, and FormulaBank-pretrained AudioMAE lifts ESC-50 from 69.50 (scratch) to 86.25 and FSD50K mAP from 0.409 to 0.565.
title: Rethinking Procedural Audio Pre-training: Source Scaling and Objective Adaptation (Peng et al., 2026; newer than my training data, verify)
relevance: Hyperparameters inherited from natural-image recipes (augmentation strength, temperature, mask ratio) can be wrong for a low-entropy synthetic source; HyperNet's first-epoch information loss is consistent with an objective that is too easy on clean drawings. If v0.4 uses reconstruction or contrastive losses, their difficulty should be set from the synthetic source's own entropy, and class coverage and member diversity should be scaled as separate axes.

claim: When the downstream prior must handle noise rather than object identity, 1/f^alpha spectral noise is the best synthetic pretraining source and unstructured noise the worst: for implicit-neural-representation denoising on CelebA-HQ, Snp-Spectrum 27.6 dB PSNR vs Siren 28.3, Strainer (real data) 27.3, Snp-Uniform 23.0, Snp-Gaussian 23.8; dead leaves falls in between; on OASIS-MRI fitting, noise pretraining (79.3 dB) beats real-data pretraining (62.8-67.0) and random init (53.03).
title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Noise Pretraining for Implicit Neural Representations (Vyas et al., CVPR 2026; newer than my training data, verify)
relevance: Gravity Spy backgrounds are colored detector noise with a steep spectrum; a synthetic prior that includes 1/f^alpha backgrounds (with alpha sampled over a range) teaches the network what 'nothing' looks like, which is the first requirement for driving false alarms below the ~90 per 10,000 all current methods show.

claim: Formula-driven and fractal pretraining transfer to grayscale scientific/medical imagery at parity with ImageNet: fractal self-supervised pretraining matched or exceeded ImageNet pretraining for early-stage lung-cancer CT GTV segmentation (2025), and FDIF (signed-distance-function volumes, no real data, 2026) outperforms the prior formula-driven method on AMOS, ACDC and KiTS and is comparable to self-supervised pretraining on large real datasets.
title: Fractal-driven self-supervised learning enhances early-stage lung cancer GTV segmentation (2025); FDIF listing at https://www.catalyzex.com/paper/fdif-formula-driven-supervised-learning-with (2026); both newer than my training data, verify
relevance: Supports the project premise that synthetic-only pretraining can work on non-photographic grayscale data, but all these results use fine-tuning with real labels; none tests frozen features with one labeled reference, which remains HyperNet's unaddressed regime.

claim: Certain convolutional pooling architectures are inherently frequency selective and translation invariant with random weights, and a large fraction of the performance of state-of-the-art feature-learning methods is attributable to the architecture alone, so random-weight performance can rank architectures without training.
title: On Random Weights and Unsupervised Feature Learning (Saxe, Koh, Chen, Bhand, Suresh, Ng)
relevance: Explains why HyperNet's random fine/middle/coarse blocks on a 6x6 grid score 0.51-0.54 DEV AP: the conv+pool structure plus fixed Sobel/contrast channels already gives band-pass, shift-tolerant features that spectrogram glitches need. The 0.388 random vs 0.219 trained result is the Saxe effect, not a bug.

claim: On audio spectrograms, randomly weighted CNN features with a linear/SVM readout beat MFCC baselines and reach a large fraction of trained-CNN accuracy: GTZAN 59.65% (random VGG+SVM) vs 53.44% MFCC vs 82.1% trained; Extended Ballroom 89.82% vs 63.25% vs 93.7%; UrbanSound8K 70.74% vs 65.49% vs 73%.
title: Randomly weighted CNNs for (music) audio classification (Pons, Serra)
relevance: Direct precedent that untrained CNN features are a strong spectrogram baseline. HyperNet's v0.2/v0.3 random-readout numbers are consistent with this literature; the README can cite it to show the random baseline is expected, not a protocol failure.

claim: A randomly weighted Wide ResNet-50 contains an untrained subnetwork (30% of weights, Signed Kaiming Constant init) that reaches 73.3% ImageNet top-1, matching a trained ResNet-34; random ResNet-101 subnetwork reaches 72.3%; the random distribution matters (Kaiming Normal 67.95% vs Signed Kaiming Constant 73.3% for WRN-50).
title: What's Hidden in a Randomly Weighted Neural Network? (Ramanujan et al., CVPR 2020)
relevance: Random weights contain enough diverse filters that selection alone (not weight change) can solve hard tasks; the choice of init distribution shifts results by 5-7 points. For v0.4: try several init seeds/distributions for the random readout and treat the seed as a hyperparameter selected on DEV only, since random-feature quality is not a single number.

claim: Deep networks have a critical period: Fisher information between layers rises rapidly in the first epochs then decreases ('Information Plasticity'), strong connections formed early 'do not appear to change during additional training', and the initial learning transient largely determines the final outcome; deficits that preserve low-level image statistics (e.g. vertical flip) cause no lasting damage.
title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Networks (Achille, Rovere, Soatto)
relevance: Matches HyperNet's observation that final-embedding AP falls from 0.432 to 0.17-0.22 after epoch 1 and never recovers in deeper blocks (only run01's fine block recovers). The first epoch commits the middle/coarse blocks to the synthetic drawing statistics. Implication: any fix must act at epoch 0 (data distribution, objective), not later fine-tuning.

claim: Most of the structural change in a network happens in the earliest iterations/epochs: weight distributions become highly non-independent after only a few hundred iterations, networks are not robust to re-randomizing weights while keeping signs, and blurred inputs or a self-supervised auxiliary task reproduce the same early changes without labels (labels only speed it up).
title: The Early Phase of Neural Network Training (Frankle, Schwab, Morcos)
relevance: Confirms that a label-free contrastive objective is sufficient to cause the early irreversible change HyperNet sees. HyperNet's 2,688 steps per run is well past the few-hundred-iteration window, so logging per-layer DEV AP every ~50 steps during epoch 1 would locate exactly when spectrogram information is lost.

claim: In sufficiently deep networks the early layers build linearly separable features while the later layers ('the tunnel') compress representations, add little in-distribution, degrade out-of-distribution generalization, and this tunnel appears early in training; OOD probe performance tracks the numerical rank of the representation, and the last layer before the tunnel is the best place for a linear probe on external data.
title: The Tunnel Effect: Building Data Representations in Deep Neural Networks (Masarczyk et al., NeurIPS 2023)
relevance: The closest published analogue of HyperNet's depth-ordered damage (stem OK, fine -0.12, middle -0.20, coarse -0.26). For v0.4: measure effective rank of each block's features on DEV spectrograms at epoch 0/1/12; if rank collapses in fine/middle/coarse, the tunnel-effect diagnosis is confirmed and the fix is to keep the pre-tunnel readout and/or reduce depth or compression pressure.

claim: The tunnel effect is not universal: training on high-resolution datasets with many classes greatly reduces representation compression in deep layers and improves OOD transferability; the effect is tied to intermediate neural collapse and depends on architecture, data, resolution and augmentation.
title: What Variables Affect Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Pretrained Models? (Harun et al.)
relevance: HyperNet trains at 96 px on a limited number of synthetic families per run with a family-classification head, which is the regime (low resolution, few effective classes, low diversity) where compression and OOD loss are worst. Suggests v0.4 variables: many more families (v15's million-family curriculum), higher render resolution, and removing the family-classification head.

claim: Contrastive learning exhibits dimensional collapse (embeddings occupy a low-dimensional subspace), driven by strong augmentation along feature dimensions and by implicit regularization in over-parameterized projectors; removing the trainable projector and feeding a subvector of the representation to the loss (DirectCLR) outperforms SimCLR with a linear projector on ImageNet.
title: Understanding Dimensional Collapse in Contrastive Self-supervised Learning (Jing, Vincent, LeCun, Tian, ICLR 2022)
relevance: HyperNet's InfoNCE on global embeddings plus a VICReg-style variance/covariance term (part_encoder_v2.py, weight 5 on variance, 1 on covariance) is applied to the 128-D 'raw' projection, so it protects the embedding's rank but not the rank of the fine/middle/coarse feature maps where the damage is. v0.4 could apply the variance/covariance penalty to pooled block features, or report per-block singular-value spectra as a diagnostic.

claim: Contrastive models become invariant to the augmentations they are trained with, these learned invariances strongly affect downstream performance, and different downstream tasks benefit from opposite (in)variances, so the standard augmentation recipe causes performance loss on some tasks; fusing representations with complementary invariances transfers broadly.
title: Why Do Self-Supervised Models Transfer? Investigating the Impact of Invariance on Downstream Tasks (Ericsson, Gouk, Hospedales)
relevance: Spectrograms are not invariant to vertical shift (frequency), affine warps or flips; HyperNet's two renders differ by exactly such transforms, so the network learns to discard the cues that separate glitch classes (e.g. Whistle vs Scattered Light differ by frequency location and slope). This is the mechanism behind 'trained features are more position sensitive at large shifts but worse at ranking'. v0.4: audit the augmentation set against the physics of glitch classes and keep an early-layer (less invariant) readout in a fused descriptor.

claim: Contrastive pretraining on purely synthetic/noise images transfers to real data in proportion to the diversity and structural statistics of the generator, not its realism: on ImageNet-100 linear probe (AlexNet) random CNN 0.21, FractalDB 0.33, dead-leaves textures 0.41, StyleGAN oriented 0.43, Places 0.55, ImageNet-100 0.63; recall/log-volume diversity correlate with accuracy (r about 0.79-0.83), colour similarity to natural images correlates negatively (r = -0.57), and perceptual variation between the two crops of a positive pair has a sweet spot near 0.37.
title: Learning to See by Looking at Noise (Baradad, Wulff, Wang, Isola, Torralba, NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: The strongest positive precedent for HyperNet's premise: synthetic-only contrastive pretraining CAN beat random features by a wide margin, but only when the synthetic distribution is diverse and has oriented, wavelet-like, textured statistics. HyperNet's shape-family drawings (clean strokes, masks) are closer to the low-diversity end. v0.4 should add dead-leaves/texture/noise-background generators and tune positive-pair dissimilarity, and report the diversity metrics the paper uses.

claim: Formula-driven fractal pretraining (no natural images) improves fine-tuning over scratch on most benchmarks (CIFAR-10 93.4 vs 87.6; CIFAR-100 75.7 vs 62.7; Omniglot 20.9 vs 1.1) but is worse than scratch on ImageNet-1k (70.3 vs 76.1), and fully randomized labels make training fail entirely; well-defined, balanced categories are required.
title: Pre-training without Natural Images (Kataoka et al.)
relevance: Shows synthetic pretraining can hurt relative to scratch on some targets (IN1k) while helping others, and that the category structure of the synthetic data is what carries the benefit. HyperNet's family-classification loss over procedural programs is a FractalDB-style objective; its category definition (one program instance = one family) is the weak point the v15 scope review names.

claim: Deep ReLU networks learn low-frequency components of a target first regardless of amplitude, and high-frequency components are significantly less robust to parameter perturbation; the deep image prior's convolutional architecture fits low-frequency structured content before noise, so an untrained conv generator is already a low-level image prior and early stopping acts as a low-pass filter.
title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks (Rahaman et al., ICML 2019); see also The Spectral Bias of the Deep Image Prior https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08905 and Deep Image Prior https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.10925
relevance: Explains why the random network is a good spectrogram prior (stationary-GP-like, band-pass) but does NOT explain the depth gradient of HyperNet's damage; spectral bias would hurt all layers roughly alike. Treat spectral bias as the reason random is strong, and the tunnel/invariance mechanisms as the reason trained is weak. Low confidence that fine-tuning schedule tweaks (early stopping) fix it, since the loss is already present after epoch 1.

claim: Joint time-frequency scattering (a convolutional network with fixed wavelet filters and no learning) beats delta-MFCC and time scattering on three audio tasks and matches or beats CNNs on two: TIMIT phone error 15.7% (JTFS) vs 17.3% time scattering vs 18.3% MFCC vs 11.9% CNN; Medley-solos-DB instrument error 22.0% vs 38.0% vs 39.3% vs 26.0% (spiral CNN); DCASE2013 scene error 5% vs 12% vs 42% vs 7% (L3 network).
title: Joint Time-Frequency Scattering (Anden, Lostanlen, Mallat; IEEE TSP 2019)
relevance: A principled fixed extractor (Kymatio implements it, arXiv 1812.11214) that encodes exactly the chirp/modulation structure glitch classes differ by. A 2-D scattering (J=2-3, L=8) on the 140x170 crop is a natural v0.4 control alongside raw pixels and the random readout; if it beats 0.572 mean AP, the bar for any learned feature rises.

claim: Applied directly to Gravity Spy v1.1.0 spectrogram data (21 usable classes, 70/15/15 split, random-forest classifier), Kymatio wavelet scattering (J=7, 7 angles, orders 1+2, Morlet) gives 88.57% test accuracy vs 87.41% for the Q-transform image and 91.03% when both are merged; WST on GPU is about 3.35x faster than the GWpy Q-transform (0.063 s vs 0.211 s per sample).
title: Wavelet Scattering Transform for Gravitational Waves Analysis. An Application to Glitch Characterization (Licciardi, Carbone, Rondoni, Nagar)
relevance: The only paper found that applies a scattering transform to the same Gravity Spy spectrograms. It is a supervised 21-class result, not one-reference retrieval, so numbers are not comparable to mean AP, but it establishes WST as a strong, fixed, physics-motivated feature on this exact data. v0.4 should add a WST (first-order, J around 3-4 on the 140x170 image, or on the Q-transform image) readout under the frozen one-reference protocol as a baseline, and can reuse their J/angle settings.

claim: First-layer conv features are general (Gabor-like filters, colour blobs) across datasets, while deeper layers become task-specific; transferability drops with task distance, but transferring from even distant tasks still beat random filters in the deep AlexNet/ImageNet setting, whereas earlier small-network studies found random filters nearly as good as learned ones.
title: How transferable are features in deep neural networks? (Yosinski, Clune, Bengio, Lipson, NeurIPS 2014)
relevance: Explains the stem's immunity (+0.004): it sits on fixed Sobel/contrast channels and learns generic edge/blob detectors that any image task reuses. It also warns that random beating trained is the expected regime for small networks and distant domains; HyperNet (755k params, drawings to spectrograms) is squarely that regime, so the comparison to make is random vs trained-on-diverse-data, not random vs the current curriculum.

claim: Zenodo 5649212 (v1.0.0, CC BY 4.0, 742.2 MB) holds Gravity Spy ML classifications for every Omicron trigger with SNR>7.5 and peak frequency 10-2048 Hz from O1, O2, O3a and O3b, as eight CSVs (H1/L1 x run; L1_O3b.csv is 216.1 MB, L1_O3a.csv 142.3 MB, H1_O3b.csv 111.6 MB) with columns event_time, peak_time, peak_time_ns, start_time, duration, peak_frequency, snr, gravityspy_id, 22 per-class confidences, ml_label, ml_confidence and url1-url4 (0.5/1/2/4 s omega scans).
title: Gravity Spy Machine Learning Classifications of LIGO Glitches from Observing Runs O1, O2, O3a, and O3b
relevance: This is the only public image-addressable release larger than v1.1. GPS times permit time grouping; ml_confidence permits a purity cut; url3 is the 2-second omega scan HyperNet already uses. The O3 CSVs alone give a 100k+ haystack.

claim: Glanzer et al. 2023 (the paper behind 5649212) classified 233,981 glitches from LIGO Hanford and 379,805 from LIGO Livingston through the end of O3, about 614k rows in total.
title: Data quality up to the third observing run of Advanced LIGO: Gravity Spy glitch classifications
relevance: Sets the upper bound of the haystack (~614k events, ~320k in O3) before any confidence cut.

claim: In O3, at the fiducial 90% ML confidence, the rare classes have very few events: Chirp 8 (H1) + 12 (L1), Wandering Line 10 + 28, Helix 15 + 37, Paired Doves 29 + 277, 1400 Ripples 85 + 2,384; at 95% the numbers fall to Chirp 5+8, Wandering Line 5+20, Helix 9+16, Paired Doves 12+130, 1400 Ripples 49+1,479.
title: Data quality up to the third observing run of Advanced LIGO: Gravity Spy glitch classifications (full text)
relevance: A fresh O3 test set can be stratified for Paired Doves and 1400 Ripples (mostly from L1) but Chirp and Wandering Line will have ~20-40 positives at most even using both detectors and both O3 halves; plan intervals accordingly or treat them as 'few-positive' targets. These counts are machine labels, not human-verified.

claim: Zenodo 5911227 (CC BY 4.0, one 1.1 GB HDF5, key 'image_db') gives, for every O1-O3b glitch that received at least one registered-volunteer classification, the 22 ML scores, ml_label, ml_confidence, gravityspy_id, Nclassifications, final_score, final_label and a 'retired' flag computed with min 2 volunteer classifications, max 50, and >0.9 class posterior weighted by ML scores.
title: Gravity Spy Volunteer Classifications of LIGO Glitches from Observing Runs O1, O2, O3a, and O3b
relevance: Joining this on gravityspy_id with the 5649212 CSVs yields human+machine agreed labels for a fresh TEST set (require retired==1 and final_label==ml_label and ml_confidence>=0.95). It contains no image URLs or times, so the CSVs remain necessary.

claim: gwpy's GravitySpyTable.download(download_path='download', parallel=1, download_durs=(0.5,1.0,2.0,4.0), training_set=False, labelled_samples=False) fetches the PNGs named in url1-url4 (skipping rows where url1 is empty or '?') and saves them as {ifo}_{gravityspy_id}_spectrogram_{duration}.png; the older keyword nproc has been renamed parallel; GravitySpyTable.search() queries https://gravityspytools.ciera.northwestern.edu/search/similarity_search_restful_API/ with database 'similarity_index_o3' and era keys only up to O3b; no rate limit is documented anywhere, only a 30 s timeout.
title: gwpy/table/gravityspy.py (GravitySpyTable source) and gwpy.readthedocs.io reference
relevance: Download command: t=GravitySpyTable.read('L1_O3b.csv'); t[sel][:N].download(download_path='o3b_png', download_durs=[2.0], parallel=2). Use download_durs=[2.0] to cut volume 4x. Keep parallel small and batch, as the Zenodo page requests. The similarity search is a public trained-feature nearest-neighbour baseline HyperNet can be compared against, but only for O1-O3b ids.

claim: Gravity Spy omega-scan PNGs are 800x600 RGB with a 580x675 plot region; the v1.1 HDF5 stores a 140x170 crop of that region (crop x=[66,532], y=[105,671]).
title: Advancing glitch classification in Gravity Spy: multi-view fusion with attention-based machine learning for Advanced LIGO's fourth observing run
relevance: Images downloaded from 5649212 URLs are the same rendering as v1.1, so the existing fixed crop and 140x170 downsample (or the v15 native-crop tiling) transfer without a new preprocessing protocol.

claim: Wu et al. 2025 (O4 Gravity Spy classifier) used 8,439/1,687/3,538 train/val/test O3 glitches in 23 classes (consensus confidence >0.9, 84.5% of data) and only 2,267 early-O4 glitches (24 May - 19 Sep 2023) for confidence-distribution checks; their per-class table shows Wandering Line 25/8/25, Chirp 38/10/17, Helix 46/10/71, Paired Doves 124/31/146; the paper says improved O4 training sets are future work and points only to the existing Zenodo repositories.
title: Advancing Glitch Classification in Gravity Spy: Multi-view Fusion with Attention-based Machine Learning for Advanced LIGO's Fourth Observing Run (preprint)
year: 2024 preprint / 2025 CQG (may be newer than training data)
relevance: Confirms the O3 labelled set with 23 classes exists only inside the collaboration (not released as a split), and that no O4 labelled image set is public. Also a useful reference that supervised deep models reach only 0.74 accuracy on Wandering Line, so one-reference results on it will be noisy.

claim: Zenodo 13904422 (v1, published Nov 2024, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, 147 MB classifications.csv.bz2) contains individual volunteer classifications through 20 July 2024 with only Classification_id, Subject_id, User_hash, Anonymous_user, Workflow, Workflow_version, Timestamp and Classification; it adds 4 volunteer-only labels (70HZLINE, HIGHFREQUENCYBURST, LOWFREQUENCYBLIP, PIZZICATO) and CROWN (=Fast_Scattering), and lists 8 workflows (Level 1 with 3 classes to Level 6 with 27 classes).
title: Gravity Spy Volunteer Classifications of LIGO Glitches
relevance: Although it extends into O4 time, it has no GPS times, no gravityspy_id and no image URLs, so subjects cannot be fetched or time-grouped without a Zooniverse subject export the team does not have; and the ND licence forbids redistributing derived label tables. Not usable as a fresh test set on its own.

claim: No Gravity Spy O4 image or ML-label dataset is on Zenodo as of 2026-11-02; Zenodo searches for 'gravity spy' return only third-party 2026 records (OmegaNeuron CSVs, gwav pipeline), and the Gravity Spy blog's 2024-2026 posts mention the end of O4 (18 Nov 2025) and GWTC-4/5 releases but no new glitch dataset; a 2026 DANTE preprint cites a Zenodo DOI for an O4a dataset (10.5281/zenodo.10657991) that resolves to an unrelated record.
title: Zenodo search results for 'gravityspy'; blog.gravityspy.org; arXiv 2606.25702 (DANTE)
relevance: Do not plan on a labelled O4 Gravity Spy release; O3a/O3b from 5649212 is the freshest labelled material. Treat the DANTE DOI as unverified.

claim: The v1.1 training set (Zenodo 1486046 / concept 1476551, CC BY 4.0, 8.6 GB) has 7,966 labelled glitches in 22 classes split 5,587/1,200/1,179 by sample_type, of which 134 images (97/18/19) are blank at the floor value 0.0832, including 8 of 27 Paired Doves and 108 of 447 Extremely Loud; the original v1.0 (1476156) had 8,583 images.
title: Gravity-Spy-Glitch-Spectrogram-Classification README (third-party analysis of v1.1)
relevance: Explains the 75 'exactly constant RGB plots' v15 excluded and shows v1.1 is small (7,966) and now exhausted after three TEST uses plus v15's 4,044-event draw; the blank-image rule must be re-applied to 5649212 downloads. Note the v1.1 set was built from O1/O2 data (2018), so O3 rows are disjoint from it.

claim: Glanzer et al. do not deduplicate triggers; the same physical event can appear as several rows (three O3b candidates had two L1 triggers, S190524q had four No_Glitch triggers within a ±5 s window), and classes such as Repeating Blips and Helix occur in groups, so a fresh test set must cluster rows by event_time before sampling.
title: Data quality up to the third observing run of Advanced LIGO: Gravity Spy glitch classifications (full text)
relevance: Supports keeping v15's time-group bootstrap; recommend grouping rows within e.g. 4 s (the longest omega-scan window) per detector and sampling one row per group for TEST, while leaving all rows in the haystack.

claim: GWOSC released O4a public data (May 2023 - Jan 2024, with engineering-run periods) on 26 Aug 2025, including calibrated strain and 'auxiliary channels used for noise subtraction and detector characterization'; O3 auxiliary data (about 40 channels per LIGO detector, plus 16 extra AUX_CLN channels) are served only through NDS2 (nds.gwosc.org) and OSDF, not website download.
title: Open Data from LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA through the First Part of the Fourth Observing Run
relevance: A truly unseen, unlabeled O4a haystack can be rendered locally: fetch strain with gwpy TimeSeries.fetch_open_data('L1', t0, t1), run Omicron or a simple excess-power trigger, and render 2-s q-transform images in Gravity Spy style. No labels and a rendering style mismatch versus Panoptes PNGs, so use it for discovery, not for mAP. Auxiliary channels enable a multi-channel reference later.

claim: Gravity Spy 2.0 (NSF 2106865, live since 2023) shows volunteers glitches with auxiliary channels and collections; its datasets are available only 'from the corresponding author on reasonable request'; proprietary O4 data are available to LVK scientists; the ML training set after O3 is about 10^4 glitches in 23 classes, and the paper states Chirp and Wandering Line have few training samples.
title: Gravity Spy: Lessons Learned and a Path Forward
relevance: If the team wants O4 labels or Gravity Spy 2.0 collections, the route is an email to the Gravity Spy team (Zevin/Coughlin), not a download; budget time for that or plan without it.

claim: Zooniverse subject and classification exports (CSV with JSON metadata columns, one row per subject or classification) are generated from the Data Export tab of a project's Lab page, i.e. only by project owners/collaborators; the public Gravity Spy project pages publish no subject export.
title: Zooniverse Help: Data Exports
relevance: Rules out Zooniverse exports as a self-serve source of O4 images or of the subject_id-to-time mapping needed to use Zenodo 13904422.

claim: Under contrastive (not supervised) loss, a few easy-to-learn shared bits between the two views suppress learning of other, harder features, and augmentation is the only lever current methods have against this.
title: Intriguing Properties of Contrastive Losses (Chen & Li, NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: HyperNet's two views share the exact program geometry, an easy identity signal. This predicts the observed collapse of glitch-relevant mid-level features in epoch 1 while the stem survives. The fix is to remove the easy shared feature (independent family members as positives), not to add more augmentation.

claim: Using positives drawn from OTHER instances (nearest neighbors in a support set) instead of two augmentations of one image raised ImageNet linear accuracy from 71.7% to 75.6%, beat supervised ImageNet on 8 of 12 transfer datasets, and reduced augmentation dependence to a 2.1% relative drop with random crops only.
title: With a Little Help from My Friends: Nearest-Neighbor Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations (Dwibedi et al., ICCV 2021)
relevance: Direct evidence that cross-instance positives improve transfer and let you drop augmentations that are unsafe on spectrograms. With a generator, HyperNet can do better than NNCLR: sample true independent family members instead of estimating neighbors.

claim: Supervised contrastive learning with many positives per anchor is more stable to augmentation and optimizer choice than cross-entropy and improves robustness to natural corruptions.
title: Supervised Contrastive Learning (Khosla et al., NeurIPS 2020)
relevance: SupCon over family labels is the natural replacement for HyperNet's one-positive InfoNCE: the batch contains K independently rendered members per family and all K-1 are positives. Its reduced sensitivity to augmentation matters because HyperNet should not add crop/jitter.

claim: In cross-domain few-shot transfer, SupCon features beat cross-entropy and self-supervised MoCo-style features (5-shot mean over 12 datasets: CE 60.01, SelfSupCon 61.23, SupCon 62.79, CE+SelfSupCon 63.70), and contrastive models keep more low/mid-level information in their final layers (final-vs-initial stage CKA: CE 0.10 vs SupCon 0.12; final-stage CKA CE vs SelfSupCon 0.47).
title: A Broad Study on the Transferability of Visual Representations with Contrastive Learning (Islam et al., ICCV 2021)
relevance: Combining family-label SupCon with an instance term is the best-transferring recipe in this study; also warns that in-distribution synthetic validation accuracy will not predict Gravity Spy transfer, so DEV probes on real spectrograms must stay the selection signal.

claim: For one-shot transfer, a plain supervised embedding on base classes plus a simple classifier beats Prototypical Networks and matches MetaOptNet, and self-supervised (MoCo) embeddings are a few points worse than supervised ones from the same backbone.
title: Rethinking Few-Shot Image Classification: a Good Embedding Is All You Need? (Tian et al., ECCV 2020)
relevance: Supports making the family-classification head (over many independently-sampled families) the primary objective rather than an auxiliary; episodic/prototypical training is not needed. HyperNet's existing 'grammar' heads classify only 4 factors of one program, not independent members of thousands of families.

claim: Episodic training is unnecessary for Matching and Prototypical Networks; non-episodic (standard batch) counterparts are simpler and improve accuracy on multiple few-shot datasets.
title: On Episodes, Prototypical Networks, and Few-Shot Learning (Laenen & Bertinetto, NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: Do not build a prototypical/episodic trainer for v0.4; a nearest-class-mean readout on top of a batch-trained family embedding is the evidence-backed choice.

claim: On a small ResNet-18 trained from scratch on Tiny-ImageNet, VICReg (variance/covariance regularization) is the most augmentation-sensitive SSL method: 18.1% top-1 with weak augmentations vs 37.5% with strong, while BYOL (39.4 vs 40.1), SimCLR (39.5 vs 41.9) and SimSiam (45.6 vs 39.7) barely depend on augmentation strength.
title: FroSSL: Frobenius Norm Minimization for Efficient Multiview Self-Supervised Learning
relevance: HyperNet's loss carries a 5x variance + covariance term with effectively weak view differences (two renders). This is the regime where VICReg-style terms perform worst on a small net; reduce or replace that term and lean on family-label positives instead. DINO is also weak at this scale, so do not switch to DINO.

claim: Self-supervised features win for few-shot transfer only when the base dataset is large; with small base sets (Caltech-256, 20% of miniImageNet) they are overtaken by a supervised few-shot baseline, i.e., supervised (labelled) features are more robust to dataset size.
title: Shot in the Dark: Few-Shot Learning with No Base-Class Labels (Chen et al.)
relevance: HyperNet has free, exact family labels; the evidence says to use them as the main signal rather than relying on an instance-discrimination term, especially given the small 755k-parameter model and limited effective diversity.

claim: Contrastive pretraining on purely synthetic/noise images with MoCo v2 reaches 60.66% ImageNet-100 linear top-1 (4-Mixed), far above untrained-CNN features (10.84%) but far below real-image pretraining (ImageNet-1K 86.12%, Places 76.00%); diversity, not realism, is the key data property, and there is a sweet spot of perceptual variation.
title: Learning to See by Looking at Noise (Baradad et al., NeurIPS 2021)
relevance: Synthetic-only pretraining CAN beat random features by a wide margin on natural images, but it required a ResNet-50, strong crops, and high-diversity generators (dead-leaves occlusion, spectrum/wavelet statistics). HyperNet's 'shape family' drawings sit near the low-diversity end (Dead leaves-Shapes 38.34). Add spectrum/texture-statistics and noise-process families that look like time-frequency energy, and measure diversity.

claim: Scaling procedural generators to 21,000 short programs (executed with OpenGL) reduces the gap between real-image and procedural pretraining by 38%.
title: Procedural Image Programs for Representation Learning (Baradad et al., NeurIPS 2022)
relevance: Program-count diversity (thousands of distinct generators), not millions of parameter draws from one grammar (v15 used 1,048,576 IDs of one program family), is what moved the needle. Treat each program as a family with independently sampled members.

claim: Random-weight convolutional+pooling architectures are inherently frequency selective and translation invariant, and a surprising fraction of trained-method performance is attributable to architecture alone.
title: On Random Weights and Unsupervised Feature Learning (Saxe et al., ICML 2011)
relevance: Explains why the random middle block on a 6x6 grid (0.539) is HyperNet's best probe: frequency-selective, translation-tolerant filters are nearly the ideal spectrogram descriptor. Any new objective should be checked for preserving filter frequency diversity (e.g., track the spectrum of fine/middle filters during training); losing it is the failure to detect in epoch 1.

claim: CNNs encode absolute position mainly via zero padding/borders, and the amount of position information increases with depth (VGG single-layer probe SPC .101 at block 1 to .657 at block 5; no-padding VGG16 drops from .742 to .381).
title: How much Position Information Do Convolutional Neural Networks Encode? (Islam et al., ICLR 2020)
relevance: Consistent with HyperNet's finding that trained deep features are MORE position-sensitive than random: depth plus padding accumulates absolute position regardless of objective. Position loss is not the problem; if frequency-axis position must be kept, keep it explicitly (pooled 6x6 grid readout or coordinate channels) rather than through the loss.

claim: Invariance-only SSL discards augmentation-related information that some downstream tasks need; adding a head that predicts the transformation (E-SSL: SimCLR to 72.5% ImageNet linear; EquiMod: gains on CIFAR10 and ImageNet; LooC: separate per-augmentation embedding spaces) keeps that information without hurting invariance to the rest.
title: Equivariant Contrastive Learning / E-SSL (Dangovski et al., ICLR 2022); also EquiMod https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01244 and LooC https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.05659
relevance: If HyperNet applies any geometric nuisance between views (affine, scale, frequency shift), add a cheap head predicting the applied parameters so the mid-level features are not forced to delete scale/orientation/frequency-position, all of which separate Gravity Spy classes (e.g., Blip vs Koi Fish vs Whistle).

claim: Domain practitioners treat augmentation of glitch spectrograms as semantics-destroying: the CTSAE authors state that augmenting glitch spectrograms distorts physical meaning and chose a plain autoencoder over contrastive methods for that reason (CTSAE ARI 0.4091 / NMI 0.6362 vs DIRECT 0.2137 / 0.4281 on Gravity Spy O3).
title: CTSAE: Unsupervised Dimensionality Reduction for Clustering Gravitational Wave Glitches
relevance: Supports not adding crop/color/flip augmentations in v0.4 and favoring generator-side variation (independent family members) over image-side augmentation. Also a candidate comparison point if unlabeled in-domain pretraining is later allowed (open problem 4).

claim: In music spectrogram SSL, pitch-shift augmentation alters properties essential for key detection; a masking-only contrastive model that avoids such augmentations reaches 68.6 on the GiantSteps key benchmark vs 14.9 for augmentation-based CLMR (different models/data, not a controlled ablation).
title: Myna: Masking-Based Contrastive Learning of Musical Representations
relevance: Frequency-axis shifts are analogous to pitch shift; a glitch's absolute frequency band is class-defining. If a second view is needed beyond independent family members, use time/frequency masking rather than frequency shifts, crops or jitter. 2025 paper, may be newer than training data; verify details.

claim: In astronomy-image contrastive learning with 845,254 unlabeled images, Gaussian noise injection was the most useful augmentation and PSF blur the weakest; the resulting linear classifier needs roughly 16x fewer labels than supervised training for Galaxy Zoo question 1.
title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Astronomical Images (Hayat et al., ApJL 2021)
relevance: Physics-motivated noise augmentation transfers to scientific images; a time-frequency noise-floor model (whitened Gaussian background, variable SNR) is the safest view-generating nuisance for spectrograms. Also the best-documented precedent for open problem 4 (unlabeled in-domain SSL) should that be permitted.

claim: Dimensional collapse in contrastive learning has two causes, strong augmentation along feature dimensions and implicit low-rank regularization in over-parameterized networks; removing the trainable projector (DirectCLR) gives 62.7% vs 61.1% ImageNet linear at 100 epochs.
title: Understanding Dimensional Collapse in Contrastive Self-supervised Learning (Jing et al., ICLR 2022)
relevance: HyperNet's variance/covariance term targets collapse of the final raw embedding but not of the middle/coarse block features that are actually read out; log the singular-value spectrum of pooled middle-block features during training and compare to the random block as a per-epoch collapse diagnostic.

claim: Cross-domain similarity local scaling (CSLS), which subtracts from 2*cos the mean cosine of each vector to its K=10 nearest neighbours in the other set, raises nearest-neighbour retrieval P@1 by about 4-9 points over plain cosine without any labels, and the paper attributes the gain to removing hubs.
title: Word Translation Without Parallel Data (Conneau, Lample, Ranzato, Denoyer, Jegou), ICLR 2018
relevance: Directly applicable: compute the reference-by-archive cosine matrix once, subtract each archive item's mean cosine to its K nearest references/archive items and each reference's mean cosine to its K nearest archive items. Archive items that are hubs (close to every reference) are exactly the items that produce false alarms for every glitch type. Zero labels, one extra matrix op; K chosen on DEV.

claim: Mutual Proximity (global scaling) and NICDM (local scaling) reduce hubness from an average skewness of 2.5 to 0.29 (MP) and 0.94 (NICDM) across 30 public datasets with no statistically significant accuracy loss on any dataset, and in a live music recommender raised reachability of items from 72.6% to 86.2% and cut the largest hub's k=5 occurrence from 242 to 70.
title: Local and Global Scaling Reduce Hubs in Space (Schnitzer, Flexer, Schedl, Widmer), JMLR 13:2871-2902
relevance: Gives a diagnostic before any fix: compute Sk=5 (skewness of k-occurrence) on the DEV archive under raw-pixel and CNN cosine; if it is above about 1.4, hubness correction (MP or CSLS) is expected to help, if not it won't. Also the 'orphan/hub' framing predicts which archive items cause repeated false alarms across all 20 references.

claim: k-reciprocal re-ranking (keep gallery items only if the query is also in their top-k, then combine Jaccard distance of reciprocal sets with the original distance) raised mAP from 46.00 to 59.87 on Market-1501 for the IDE(R) baseline with no labels, but gave essentially zero gain on CUHK03 single-shot (mAP 63.1 -> 63.2), so the gain depends on the gallery having several true matches per query.
title: Re-ranking Person Re-identification with k-reciprocal Encoding (Zhong, Zheng, Cao, Li), CVPR 2017
relevance: Mutual-nearest-neighbour filtering is cheap on a 1,179-item archive and matches the Gravity Spy setting where each type has tens of true matches (Market-1501-like), not one (CUHK03 single-shot-like). But k1, k2, lambda are sensitive and must be fixed on DEV. Expect gains in AP; the false-alarm effect at a fixed cutoff must be measured separately.

claim: Adaptive symmetric score normalization (AS-norm: z-score each trial score against the mean and std of its top-200 most similar unlabeled cohort files on both the enrollment and test side) cut minimum DCF from 0.9539 (no normalization) to 0.6771 on NIST SRE16, about 30% relative, while the same technique with a mismatched cohort (zt-norm, NIST-only cohort) was worse than no normalization (0.9814).
title: Analysis of Score Normalization in Multilingual Speaker Recognition (Matejka, Novotny, Plchot, Burget, Diez Sanchez, Cernocky), Interspeech 2017, DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-803
relevance: The closest analogue of HyperNet's problem: one enrollment (the reference), many test items, false alarms dominated by trials whose raw score distribution is shifted. AS-norm needs only unlabeled in-domain data: the DEV archive (or the archive being searched, declared as such) serves as cohort. Use top-N (N tuned on DEV, expect a flat optimum) rather than the whole cohort, and keep the cohort in-domain (spectrograms, not synthetic drawings) or it will hurt.

claim: With a cohort restricted to the top-40 most similar impostors, adaptive s-norm reduced EER from 2.14% to 1.69% and minDCF from 0.0947 to 0.0759 (about 20% relative) when the cohort was in-domain, but an out-of-domain (VoxCeleb) cohort raised EER to 2.46% and minDCF to 0.1303, i.e. worse than no normalization.
title: Cross-Lingual Speaker Verification with Domain-Balanced Hard Prototype Mining and Language-Dependent Score Normalization (Thienpondt, Desplanques, Demuynck), Interspeech 2020
relevance: Confirms the cohort rule with a second system and embedding type (ECAPA-TDNN, cosine scoring like HyperNet). For HyperNet the cohort must be Gravity Spy spectrograms; synthetic renders as cohort would be the VoxCeleb case. The 'top-40' setting shows N can be small relative to a 1,179-item archive.

claim: OpenMax fits a per-class Weibull to the 20 largest distances between correctly classified training activations and the class mean, revises the top alpha=10 activations, and reaches F-measure 0.595 on an 80,000-image open-set test, a 4.3% gain over SoftMax at its optimal threshold; larger tail sizes reject more unknowns but also more known images, so F-measure falls.
title: Towards Open Set Deep Networks (Bendale, Boult), CVPR 2016
relevance: EVT tail fitting is a principled per-reference threshold, but the documented gain over a well-tuned global threshold is small (about 4%), and it needs tens of in-class samples per class to fit the tail, which one reference does not provide. The usable variant is fitting the Weibull/GPD to the impostor (non-match) tail of each reference's normalized scores on the unlabeled DEV archive, which needs no labels.

claim: SPOT sets a detection threshold z_q from a Generalized Pareto fit to peaks over an initial threshold so that P(X > z_q) < q for a user-chosen risk q, needs only an initial batch of about n=1000 values, converges to the true quantile (3.09 for q=1e-3 on Gaussian noise), and on a SYN-flood stream at q=1e-4 gave 86% true positive rate with under 4% false positives; q between 1e-3 and 1e-5 kept high TPR and low FPR.
title: Anomaly Detection in Streams with Extreme Value Theory (Siffer, Fouque, Termier, Largouet), KDD 2017, DOI 10.1145/3097983.3098144
relevance: Gives a label-free recipe to translate 'one in 10,000' directly into a threshold: fit a GPD to the upper tail of each reference's normalized impostor scores on the unlabeled DEV archive and set z_q for q=1e-3 or 1e-4. The 4% false positive figure is per flow, not per-window, so do not quote it as a 10x reduction; the value here is the risk-parameterized threshold, which replaces the ad-hoc 1% DEV cutoff.

claim: On Gravity Spy, single-view CNNs trained on one time window reach 92.85% (0.5 s), 95.34% (1 s), 94.09% (2 s) and 93.68% (4 s) accuracy, while fusing all four windows reaches 95.75% (parallel view) and 96.89% (merged view), and individual classes favour different durations (Air Compressor 100% vs 80%, Wandering Line 57% vs 71% between the short and 4 s models).
title: Deep Multi-view Models for Glitch Classification (Bahaadini, Rohani, Coughlin, Zevin, Kalogera, Katsaggelos), ICASSP 2017
relevance: The four durations are four genuinely different views of the same event, already in the Zenodo record, so view fusion costs no labels and no new data. The error drop from 4.66% (best single view) to 3.11% (merged) is a 1.5x reduction in a supervised setting; for one-reference retrieval the per-class duration dependence suggests fusing normalized scores per view (mean or max after AS-norm) rather than concatenating features. HyperNet currently uses one 140x170 crop per event.

claim: On the O3 Gravity Spy data, attention-based intermediate fusion of the four time windows reached 0.941 accuracy / 0.931 F1 versus 0.911 / 0.901 for early fusion (views tiled into one image) and 0.922 / 0.901 for late (decision-level) fusion, on a test set of 3,538 glitches across 23 classes.
title: Advancing Glitch Classification in Gravity Spy: Multi-view Fusion with Attention-based Machine Learning for Advanced LIGO's Fourth Observing Run (Wu et al.)
relevance: Two uses: (1) late fusion of the four views is a label-free baseline that already beats tiling the views into one image, so HyperNet can fuse per-view scores without any training; (2) the O3 dataset used here (about 13,600 labelled glitches, 23 classes, confidence > 0.9) is a candidate for the fresh held-out test the project needs after three uses of TEST v1.1. Newer than some training data; verify the v2 numbers against the published version.

claim: Test-time multi-scale augmentation (descriptors at scales 1, 1/sqrt2, 1/2, GeM-pooled) raises retrieval mAP by about 2 points (Oxford5k 85.9 -> 87.9, Paris6k 86.0 -> 87.7), and alpha-weighted query expansion (alpha=3, top 50) adds a further 4 points (87.9 -> 91.9), with no labels.
title: Fine-tuning CNN Image Retrieval with No Human Annotation (Radenovic, Tolias, Chum), TPAMI 2019
relevance: Test-time augmentation is the smallest of the label-free gains (about 2 mAP points) and query expansion is risky with one reference: with only one true seed, alphaQE pulls in the top-50 neighbours which, at 90 false alarms per 10,000, include impostors, so it should be tried only after normalization and measured for false-alarm drift on DEV. Multi-scale is cheap but the Gravity Spy views already provide a multi-scale axis in time.

claim: Re-ranking the top 100 global-descriptor matches with local-feature geometric verification (RANSAC, residual threshold 20, ratio test 0.95) raised DELG mAP on Revisited Oxford Hard from 45.1 to 54.2 and on ROxford+1M Hard from 27.8 to 36.8, but only from 63.4 to 64.9 on Revisited Paris Hard.
title: Unifying Deep Local and Global Features for Image Search (Cao, Araujo, Sim), ECCV 2020
relevance: Geometric verification helps most when the global descriptor is weakest (Hard, +1M distractors), which is HyperNet's regime, but it presumes repeatable keypoints under a rigid transform. Spectrogram glitches of one type are not geometrically aligned instances, so a direct port is unlikely; the transferable idea is a second, independent verifier on the top-k (e.g. translation-search matching of the time-frequency patch, which v15 already has) applied as a cascade stage after a cheap normalized-cosine shortlist.

claim: In a cascaded detector the overall false-positive rate is the product of the per-stage rates, so ten stages each passing 30% of negatives give about 6e-6 overall while ten stages each keeping 99% of positives retain about 90% recall; the original Viola-Jones face detector used 38 stages.
title: Face Detection and Recognition lecture notes (University of Washington CSE 576), citing Viola and Jones 2001
relevance: The only mechanism in this list that routinely delivers 100x-1000x false-alarm reduction, but every stage costs some recall and needs a verifier whose errors are not the same as the previous stage's. For HyperNet a two-stage cascade (normalized CNN cosine shortlist, then v15's translation-search matcher on the shortlist) is feasible without labels; the recall cost per stage must be measured on DEV.

claim: If zero events are observed in n independent trials, the 95% upper confidence bound on the event rate is about 3/n (exactly -ln(0.05)/n = 2.996/n), good for n > 30.
title: Rule of three (statistics), Wikipedia
relevance: Sets the honest-measurement floor. On 1,179 TEST items, 90 per 10,000 is about 11 false alarms; the smallest non-zero rate observable is 8.5 per 10,000, and zero false alarms only proves a rate below 25 per 10,000. A claimed 10x reduction therefore cannot be demonstrated on TEST v1.1 at all; it needs the fresh 4,044-event set (zero events bounds the rate below 7.4 per 10,000) or pooled O3 data, and per-type false-alarm counts should be reported with binomial (Clopper-Pearson) intervals rather than a single rate.

claim: Speaker-recognition evaluations report an actual detection cost at a threshold fixed before scoring and separately a minimum cost at the best post-hoc threshold; the threshold is either the Bayes threshold for calibrated scores or tuned on a supervised calibration set, and the gap between actual and minimum cost is the standard measure of calibration failure, which in one SRE 2010 system report broke down at operating points with fewer than about 30 false alarms.
title: The BOSARIS Toolkit: Theory, Algorithms and Code for Surviving the New DCF (Brummer, de Villiers)
relevance: Template for the v0.4 protocol: declare the DEV-chosen cutoff (and any AS-norm N, CSLS K, fusion weights) in protocol.json before TEST, report recall at that fixed cutoff as the primary number (the 'actual' cost) and recall at the best TEST cutoff only as a secondary 'minimum' number, and treat a large gap as evidence the DEV calibration did not transfer. The 30-false-alarm breakdown warns that calibrating a 1-in-10,000 operating point on a 1,179-item DEV set is itself unreliable.

claim: Reusing one holdout set for adaptively chosen hypotheses leads to overfitting to the holdout set itself; validity needs either a fresh set or a noise-adding reuse mechanism.
title: Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse (Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, Roth)
relevance: TEST v1.1 has been scored three times (v0.1, v0.2, v0.3) and each round chose the next experiment after seeing TEST. Even with frozen protocols the TEST numbers are now mildly optimistic for the selected method. The final write-up should state the number of TEST uses and what each use informed, and confirm the headline comparisons once on a fresh set.

claim: Empirically, adaptive overfitting from test-set reuse is small when a final held-out set is used once: across 100+ Kaggle competitions public-vs-private leaderboard gaps showed 'little evidence of substantial overfitting', and on ImageNet/CIFAR new test sets caused 3-15% (CIFAR-10) and 11-14% (ImageNet) accuracy drops that the authors attribute to distribution shift, not adaptivity, with model rankings preserved.
title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet? (Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt, Shankar, ICML 2019); A Meta-Analysis of Overfitting in Machine Learning (Roelofs et al., NeurIPS 2019, https://papers.nips.cc/paper/9117-a-meta-analysis-of-overfitting-in-machine-learning)
relevance: The bigger risk for HyperNet is not that three uses inflated 0.572, but that a fresh Gravity Spy sample (different observing run, different glitch rates, O3-only classes) will shift all methods. The write-up should report old-TEST vs fresh-TEST side by side for every arm (trained, random, raw pixels) and treat the gap as a measured quantity, as v15 already saw when raw48 scored 19.7% on 4,044 fresh events.

claim: Even a researcher who runs exactly one analysis faces a multiple-comparisons problem when the choice of that analysis depends on the data; the remedy is to fix analysis details before seeing the data (preregistration) or to analyse all potential comparisons.
title: The garden of forking paths: Why multiple comparisons can be a problem, even when there is no 'fishing expedition' or 'p-hacking' and the research hypothesis was posited ahead of time (Gelman and Loken)
relevance: HyperNet's protocol.json with SHA-256 written before TEST scoring is exactly the preregistered-phi case. The final write-up should list, per benchmark version, what was frozen (references, candidate readouts, selection rule, metric definitions, bootstrap unit, number of draws) and when, and should note the one forking point that remains: the all-random four-layer mix was best on DEV but excluded by a rule that required a trained block. Report both the rule-selected and the overall-best DEV readouts on TEST.

claim: The NeurIPS 2020 Preregistration Workshop exists because ML rewards only positive results and omits negative ones; a preregistered paper is reviewed on protocol before results, then experiments are reported regardless of outcome (73 proposals, 38 accepted, 23 results papers published).
title: Preface, NeurIPS 2020 Workshop on Pre-registration in Machine Learning (PMLR 148)
relevance: This is the template for presenting a negative result: write the fresh-TEST protocol as a short preregistration document (hypotheses, arms, metrics, selection rule, stopping rule), timestamp/hash it, then present results as 'confirmatory'. Citing this workshop also gives STS judges a recognized ML venue that treats negative preregistered findings as publishable.

claim: Kapoor and Narayanan found leakage errors in 329 papers across 17 fields and name eight leakage types, including [L1.4] duplicates in datasets, [L3.1] temporal leakage and [L3.2] nonindependence between training and test samples; when errors were corrected, complex ML models did not beat logistic regression.
title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science (Kapoor and Narayanan, Patterns 2023; arXiv 2207.07048)
relevance: HyperNet's leakage exposure is L1.4/L3.2 (the same glitch rendered at 0.5/1/2/4 s and near-simultaneous Omicron triggers) and L3.1 (reference and test drawn from the same hours of detector state). The write-up should include a model-info-sheet style section: how references were chosen, how many TEST events share a time group with a reference, and that no gradient ever touched a spectrogram. Also, the paper's headline (simple baselines win once leakage is removed) frames raw-pixels-beats-CNN as a known pattern rather than an embarrassment.

claim: Published Gravity Spy ML papers split the dataset randomly or by glitch subject, never by time: Zevin et al. 2017 used 75%/12.5%/12.5% train/validation/test of ~7,718 O1 glitches in 20 classes; Wu et al. 2024 used 8,439/1,687/3,538 glitches 'selected randomly' with 'no overlapping glitch subjects'.
title: Gravity Spy: Integrating Advanced LIGO Detector Characterization, Machine Learning, and Citizen Science (Zevin et al. 2017); Advancing Glitch Classification in Gravity Spy: Multi-view Fusion (Wu et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/html/2401.12913); Gravity Spy Training Set v1.1.0 (https://zenodo.org/records/1486046)
relevance: No published Gravity Spy split handles temporal proximity, so HyperNet cannot inherit a time-safe split from the dataset and should build its own: group TEST events by ifo and event_time (e.g. any two triggers within the 4 s window, or a conservative 10-60 s) and never let a reference's group appear among its own candidates. Report the count of such groups. The v15 benchmark already did this (4,044 events in 3,954 time groups); v0.1-v0.3 should state whether they did.

claim: Gravity Spy's own lessons-learned paper flags class imbalance, rare classes with very few examples, noisy training labels derived partly from ML, and the difficulty of 'four versions of the same glitch images in different time durations' as structural weaknesses of the training set.
title: Gravity Spy: Lessons Learned and a Path Forward (Zevin et al., Eur. Phys. J. Plus 139, 100)
relevance: Mean AP over 20 classes gives a class with 4 positives the same weight as one with 300, and label noise caps attainable AP. The write-up should give per-class positive counts in TEST, report Rare-AP separately (already done) with its own interval, and treat labels as noisy upper bounds. Using one duration only (the 2 s crop) and grouping by gravityspy_id removes the four-versions duplicate path.

claim: On imbalanced data ROC-style summaries stay unchanged while precision collapses: in Saito and Rehmsmeier's simulation the same operating point gives 160 FP/500 TP (75% precision) balanced but 1,600 FP/500 TP (25% precision) at 1:10 imbalance, and in a reanalysis a tool with ROC AUC 0.886 had PR AUC 0.054; they 'strongly recommend PRC plots'.
title: The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets (Saito and Rehmsmeier, PLOS ONE 10(3) e0118432)
relevance: Mean AP (area under PR) is the right primary metric and the chance level (0.049) should always be printed next to it. v15's mean AUROC of ~0.79 alongside 3.6% recall is a live example of the ROC-looks-fine trap; the write-up should lead with AP and recall-at-cutoff, and show AUROC only as a secondary number with this caveat.

claim: Recall at a fixed false-alarm rate is the standard operating-point metric in rare-match benchmarks, but very low rates are only estimable with very large negative sets: IJB-C reports TAR at FAR 1e-4/1e-5 (and 1e-6 on MegaFace) because its 1:1 protocol has about 15.6 million impostor pairs versus ~19,500 genuine pairs.
title: MixFaceNets: Extremely Efficient Face Recognition Networks (Boutros et al.), with SphereFace2 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.01513) and EPL (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.12447) as corroborating examples
